specPoints.text: describe the role of the placenta in the nutrition of the developing embryo

primer.text: A fetus cannot eat, breathe or excrete — yet it grows. Its delivery service is the placenta: a thin-walled, wide-surfaced exchange post where maternal and fetal blood run close enough to swap oxygen and nutrients for carbon dioxide and urea without ever mixing, while the umbilical cord links the trade route to the fetus.

lessons.title: The Exchange Service Between Two Bloods
lessons.opening: After implantation the placenta forms and becomes the fetus's lifeline: mother's blood and fetal blood flow close together but never mix, oxygen and nutrients cross toward the fetus while carbon dioxide and urea cross back, and the umbilical cord carries the exchange to the fetus.
keyPoints: After the embryo settles into the uterine lining, the placenta forms at that landing site.
The placenta is the exchange point where substances cross between maternal blood and fetal blood.
Oxygen and nutrients such as glucose, amino acids and vitamins pass to the fetus.
Carbon dioxide and urea pass from the fetus's blood to the mother.
The two blood supplies stay separate; the umbilical cord links fetus to placenta.

low.restatement: Food and oxygen in, waste out — through one organ, with the two bloods kept apart by a thin wall.
low.analogy: A border market where traders exchange goods across a counter without ever entering each other's country.
low.examPointer: Always state the direction of travel for each substance — the exam hint singles this out.

medium.restatement: The placenta earns its exchange title structurally: a large surface area and a thin wall shorten every diffusion path, and while some toxins slip past — nicotine, alcohol and virus particles included — it still blocks many pathogens from reaching the fetus.
medium.analogy: A sieve-like customs wall: fast trade for essentials, a partial filter for smugglers.
medium.examPointer: Mention large surface area and thin wall when asked why the placenta is efficient.

options.text: Where the embryo settles into the uterine lining
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: In the oviduct after fertilisation
options.explanation: The oviduct hosts fertilisation; the placenta forms later in the uterus.

options.text: Inside the ovary
options.explanation: The ovary releases eggs; no placenta forms there.

options.text: Along the umbilical cord only
options.explanation: The cord connects to the placenta; it is not the organ itself.

check.stem: Which substances cross the placenta toward the fetus?

options.text: Oxygen and nutrients such as glucose, amino acids and vitamins
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and urea
options.explanation: Those travel the opposite way, fetus to mother.

options.text: Urea and minerals only
options.explanation: Urea is fetal waste leaving, not arriving.

options.text: Antibodies only
options.explanation: Antibodies may cross, but the taught pair is oxygen and nutrients.

check.stem: Why is it vital that the mother's blood and the fetus's blood do not mix?

options.text: Exchange happens across the thin placental wall without the two supplies combining
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Mixing would add chromosomes to the fetus
options.explanation: Blood mixing does not alter the fetal genome.

options.text: The mother's blood would digest the fetus
options.explanation: Digestion is not the taught risk.

options.text: Mixing is impossible physically
options.explanation: The systems stay separate by design, not impossibility.

check.stem: Which two structural features make the placenta an efficient exchange surface?

options.text: A large surface area and a thin wall for diffusion
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: A thick wall and a small surface
options.explanation: Both would slow exchange.

options.text: Valves and a pump
options.explanation: The placenta has no pump; hearts drive the flow.

options.text: Cilia and mucus
options.explanation: Ciliated linings belong to airways and oviducts.

check.stem: A pregnant woman smokes. What does the barrier behaviour of the placenta predict?

options.text: Nicotine can cross the placenta and reach the fetus, since not all toxins are stopped
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.

options.text: The placenta filters every chemical perfectly
options.explanation: Nicotine, alcohol and viruses pass through.

options.text: Smoke improves nutrient transfer
options.explanation: Smoking harms, not helps, the exchange.

options.text: The umbilical cord blocks all drugs
options.explanation: The cord is a conduit, not a filter.

check.stem: Name the structure connecting the fetus's blood supply to the placenta.
check.modelAnswer: The umbilical cord connects the fetus's blood supply to the placenta.

check.stem: State two waste substances that pass from fetal blood to maternal blood.
check.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide and urea pass from the fetus's blood to the mother.

check.stem: Explain why the placenta's large surface area and thin wall matter for the fetus.
check.modelAnswer: A large surface area gives more room for exchange and a thin wall shortens the diffusion distance, so oxygen and nutrients reach the fetus quickly and wastes leave equally fast.

check.stem: Write a four-mark answer describing how the placenta serves the fetus.
check.modelAnswer: The placenta supplies the fetus with oxygen plus nutrients — glucose, amino acids and the rest — while shipping out carbon dioxide and urea, with the exchange happening by diffusion across its thin, wide wall.

glossary.definition: The structure at the implantation site that exchanges substances between mother and fetus.
The cord connecting the fetus's blood supply to the placenta.
The settling of the embryo into the uterine lining, where the placenta forms.

figures.alt: Diagram of placenta showing a cross-section with labelled parts: placenta, placental membrane, villi, umbilical cord, foetus and mother's blood vessels.
